correctness.rationale: The 13 divisor classes are explicitly defined on the 6-point blowup, whose intersection form reconstructs exactly 21 distinct transverse ordinary nodes and genus 9. The 13x13 Laplacian splits by the K4 vertex/edge/matching incidence identities into a 3x3 constant block, three 2x2 standard blocks and two 2x2 matching blocks, yielding the exact characteristic polynomial. Matrix-tree gives order 7^3*13^2; reductions modulo 7 and 13 give reduced nullities 3 and 2, which force all prime-primary factors to have exponents 7 and 13. Standalone Python standard-library verification reconstructs the geometry, matrix, integer characteristic polynomial, three rooted determinants and modular ranks. The Neron statement is conditional on a proper regular split semistable smoothing with unit node thicknesses and follows from Raynaud's theorem. No assertion about arbitrary smoothings or positive-characteristic degenerations.

Targeted published-finding corpus and public literature queries for aliases, group order, Smith invariants, and Cayley graph returned no covering indexed result. This is a positive statement-versus-statement comparison, not an inference of uniqueness from search failure; an unindexed historical calculation is a residual risk.

value.rationale: The reduced union of all thirteen negative curves is the canonical complete negative-curve boundary of the unique four-nodal cubic's minimal resolution, with genus 9. Its exact component group is an arithmetic degeneration invariant of a geometrically distinguished surface, not a cherry-picked subgraph. The 7-primary rank three and 13-primary rank two are integral data not recoverable from the spanning-tree order or rational Laplacian spectrum alone, and are potentially useful for comparing semistable Jacobian degenerations and integral graph-lattice behavior. The prior Cayley Zariski-chamber count and Cox-ring tables do not give this finite group. This finite exact classification is motivated independently of the computation and does not assert a broader downstream theorem.
